howItWorks.intro: Gas cost isn't looked up from a table — it's assembled from the actual EVM operations your transaction triggers, then priced in ETH and converted to dollars. Below is the exact arithmetic this calculator runs on the numbers you enter.

rules.name: Gas Cost
rules.formula: Cost (USD) = Gas Units x Gas Price (Gwei) / 1e9 x ETH Price
rules.explanation: Convert gas units to ETH using the gas price, then multiply by the current ETH/USD exchange rate.

howItWorks.outro: Because gas price is negotiated block-by-block under EIP-1559 and ETH's dollar value moves independently of network congestion, treat every result here as a snapshot, not a forecast. Re-run the calculator with the gas price shown on a live gas tracker (e.g., Etherscan's Gas Tracker or your node's eth_gasPrice) right before you sign a transaction, especially for deployments where a stale gwei estimate can throw the dollar figure off by 3-5× during congestion spikes.

faq.question: How much does it cost to deploy a smart contract?
faq.answer: It scales directly with your compiled bytecode size at 200 gas per byte, plus the 21,000-gas intrinsic transaction cost every transaction pays. A compact ERC-20 token (roughly 3,000-4,000 bytes of runtime code) typically runs 700,000-1,000,000 gas to deploy; a contract with several inherited OpenZeppelin extensions can reach 2-3 million gas. At 30 gwei and a $3,200 ETH price, a 2,421,000-gas deployment (12,000-byte contract) works out to roughly $232 — the same deployment at 80 gwei during a congested period would cost closer to $620.

faq.question: How can I reduce smart contract gas costs?
faq.answer: Pack storage variables into shared 32-byte slots instead of leaving each in its own slot, minimize SSTORE operations (a zero-to-nonzero write costs 20,000 gas versus 5,000 gas for overwriting an already-nonzero slot), replace storage-based logs with emitted events where you don't need on-chain read access, and cache repeated storage reads in memory within a function instead of re-issuing SLOAD each time. For high-frequency contracts, moving from Ethereum mainnet to an L2 rollup is usually the single biggest cost lever available.

faq.question: Why does gas price change even though I didn't change my contract?
faq.answer: Gas price is a market condition, not something a contract sets. Under EIP-1559 the base fee adjusts automatically — up or down by as much as 12.5% per block — based on how full recent blocks were relative to the 15-million-gas target, and the priority fee is whatever you or your wallet offer to compete with other pending transactions. A contract with completely unchanged logic can cost $5 to call at 2am UTC and $25 to call an hour later during a high-traffic mint, purely from network demand.

faq.question: Why do some calls to the same contract cost more gas than others?
faq.answer: Different functions execute different opcode paths. A read-only view function costs nothing when called off-chain, but a function that writes new data to storage, loops over an array, or calls out to another contract accumulates gas for each of those operations. Two functions with a similar line count in Solidity can differ by tens of thousands of gas if one touches storage (SSTORE, SLOAD) and the other only touches memory.

faq.question: Is 21,000 gas really the minimum cost for anything on Ethereum?
faq.answer: Yes — every transaction, even one sending 0 ETH with no calldata, pays the 21,000-gas intrinsic cost defined in the protocol, which covers signature verification and the base cost of block inclusion. Adding calldata bytes (4 gas per zero byte, 16 gas per non-zero byte since EIP-2028) or triggering contract execution only adds on top of that floor — it's never lower.

howWeCalculate.intro: Here's the arithmetic, worked through with realistic example numbers rather than abstractions — swap in your own contract size and current network conditions to get a live figure.
steps: Deployment gas: for a contract compiling to 12,000 bytes of runtime bytecode, the EVM charges 21,000 gas (intrinsic transaction cost) + 12,000 bytes × 200 gas/byte (codedeposit) = 2,421,000 gas — before accounting for any constructor logic that runs during deployment.

Interaction gas: a mid-complexity call — say a token swap that reads and writes two storage slots and makes one external call to a token contract — typically runs 120,000-180,000 gas. We'll use 150,000 gas as the illustrative figure below.
Convert to ETH: at a gas price of 30 gwei, that 150,000-gas swap costs 150,000 × 30 = 4,500,000 gwei, or 4,500,000 ÷ 1,000,000,000 = 0.0045 ETH.

Convert to USD: at an ETH price of $3,200, 0.0045 ETH × $3,200 = $14.40 per swap. Run the same 2,421,000-gas deployment through the same math (2,421,000 × 30 ÷ 1e9 × $3,200) and you get roughly $232.42 to deploy the contract once.
howWeCalculate.disclaimer: Gas price and ETH price are the two most volatile inputs in this formula — both can move by double-digit percentages within a single day. Treat the output as a planning estimate, and confirm against a live gas tracker before submitting a real transaction.

whenToUse.intro: Reach for this calculator at the points in a project where gas cost actually changes a decision, not just out of curiosity.
scenarios: Before choosing between deploying on Ethereum mainnet versus an L2 like Arbitrum or Base, where identical bytecode can cost 10-50× less to deploy and call.

While budgeting an audit or launch, since deploying a full protocol (factory contract plus multiple pool or vault contracts) can run into the low single-digit thousands of dollars at elevated gas prices.
When comparing two implementations of the same function — packed storage structs versus separate state variables, for example — to see the dollar impact of a gas optimization before you ship it.
Before a scheduled mint or claim event where thousands of users will call the same function within minutes, since your own users competing for block space can push gas price up sharply.
When explaining to a non-technical stakeholder why a specific transaction cost what it did, using concrete gas-unit and gwei figures instead of a vague 'gas was high' explanation.

sections.title: What Gas Units and Gas Price Actually Mean
sections.body: Every operation the Ethereum Virtual Machine executes — storing a value, reading storage, calling another contract, performing arithmetic — has a fixed gas cost defined in the protocol's opcode pricing table. Gas units aren't a currency; they're a metering unit for computational and storage work, deliberately priced so cheap operations (like ADD or PUSH, 3 gas) cost far less than expensive ones (like SSTORE writing a new storage slot, 20,000 gas, or a cold external CALL, 2,600 gas under EIP-2929). This calculator converts that raw gas figure into a dollar cost using two inputs you control: gas price in gwei (what you're willing to pay per unit of gas) and the current ETH/USD rate. The formula is Cost = Gas Units × Gas Price (gwei) ÷ 1,000,000,000 × ETH Price, since 1 gwei equals one-billionth of an ETH. Deployment gas here is driven mainly by your contract's bytecode size — the EVM charges 200 gas per byte to permanently store deployed code (the 'codedeposit' cost from the Yellow Paper), plus the flat 21,000-gas intrinsic cost every transaction pays regardless of what it does.

sections.title: Why the Gas Price Field Moves So Much
sections.body: Since the London upgrade (EIP-1559), every block carries a base fee that the protocol calculates automatically from how full the previous block was, adjusting up or down by as much as 12.5% per block toward a 15-million-gas target against a 30-million-gas block limit. That base fee is burned, not paid to anyone — it's Ethereum's way of pricing block space algorithmically instead of through a pure first-price auction. On top of it, you set a priority fee (tip) that goes directly to the block proposer to get included faster. When you enter a gas price into this calculator, you're really entering base fee plus priority fee combined. Under normal conditions that might sit around 15-30 gwei; during an NFT mint frenzy or a volatile-market liquidation cascade, tips alone can push it past 100 gwei because everyone is bidding for the same limited block space. That's why the same contract call can cost a few dollars one afternoon and several times that the next.

sections.title: Why a DeFi Swap Costs More Than a Plain Transfer
sections.body: A bare ETH transfer between two externally-owned accounts costs exactly 21,000 gas, no exceptions, because it touches no contract code. A smart contract call is different: gas accumulates for every opcode the call path executes. A typical DEX swap doesn't just move tokens — it reads reserve balances (SLOAD), updates them (SSTORE), checks the caller's ERC-20 allowance, calls transferFrom on the token contract (an external CALL with its own cold-access surcharge), and may touch a price oracle. Each of those steps adds thousands of gas, which is why a routed swap typically lands between 120,000 and 200,000 gas depending on how many liquidity pools it hops through. An NFT mint that writes an owner mapping and a token URI to storage can run anywhere from around 60,000 gas — using a gas-optimized standard like ERC721A with batch minting — up to 250,000+ gas for a naive implementation that stores full metadata on-chain per token.

howToSteps.title: Enter Contract Size in Bytes
howToSteps.description: Use the size of your compiled runtime bytecode, not your Solidity source file — pull it from your compiler's artifact output (solc --bin or Hardhat's artifacts/contracts folder). This number directly drives the 200-gas-per-byte codedeposit cost in the deployment estimate.

howToSteps.title: Set Average Daily Function Calls
howToSteps.description: Estimate how many times your contract's functions will be invoked per day after launch. This scales the daily and monthly interaction cost so you can budget ongoing operational gas spend, not just the one-time deployment.

howToSteps.title: Enter Current Gas Price in Gwei
howToSteps.description: Pull a live figure from a gas tracker or your node's eth_gasPrice call. Remember this already represents base fee plus priority fee combined under EIP-1559 — don't add them separately.

howToSteps.title: Enter ETH Price in USD
howToSteps.description: Use the current spot price. Because deployment cost multiplies a large gas figure by this number, even a 5% move in ETH's dollar value shifts your deployment budget by a proportional amount.

tips: Pull your contract's actual deployed bytecode size from your compiler output (solc --bin or Hardhat's artifacts) rather than guessing — deployment gas scales linearly with it at 200 gas per byte.
Packing multiple small state variables (two uint128 values, for example) into a single 32-byte storage slot can roughly halve your SSTORE operations compared to using separate uint256 slots.

Check whether the function you're pricing writes to a storage slot that starts at zero — the first write costs 20,000 gas, but overwriting an already-nonzero slot only costs 5,000 gas, a difference this calculator's single gas-price field won't surface on its own.
For a deployment estimate, use the gwei figure from a live gas tracker's 'safe' or 'standard' tier rather than its 'fast' tier unless you specifically need same-block inclusion.

Profile gas usage with Hardhat's gas reporter or Foundry's forge test --gas-report before deployment — it gives you exact per-function gas figures to plug into this calculator instead of rough estimates.
